title.narrative: Sustainable Wildlife Management

description.narrative: Ce programme contribuera à l'Objectif de Développement Durable (ODD 15 - Protéger, restaurer et promouvoir l'utilisation durable des écosystèmes terrestres, la gestion durable des forêts, combattre la désertification, arrêter et inverser la dégradation des terres et arrêter la perte de biodiversité). Il adresse également l'objectif 2.3 de la stratégie intra-ACP - programme indicatif 2014-2020 : Contribuer à la mise en uvre des engagements internationaux en matière denvironnement par les pays, institutions et réseaux ACP.De tout temps, les humains ont pratiqué la chasse pour répondre à leurs besoins. Aujourd'hui, les populations rurales autour du globe continuent à chasser des animaux sauvages comme source de nourriture et de revenus ainsi que pour des raisons culturelles. Au travers du commerce, les chasseurs ruraux sont reliés aux villes, où la viande sauvage est vendue. Pour les populations urbaines, la viande sauvage est moins une nécessité nutritionnelle qu'un luxe ou un festin occasionnel reliant les familles à un passé rural. Malheureusement, actuellement, presque partout où la faune est chassée pour la nourriture, l'amplitude de l'extraction dépasse le taux de reconstitution des populations de faune. En conséquence, des populations entières d'animaux sauvages terrestres à travers le monde sont en déclin ou sont éteintes (au moins localement).

comment.narrative: None of the 29 WMUs have established and implemented adaptive management rulesplans for wildlife. Approaches to adaptive management adapted to the different socioecosystems species wildlife uses and practices the community management context and the governance framework associated with the model need to be developed

This requires governance systems that are functional and fit for the specific model being developed. At most sites except Guyana efforts to develop those governance systems began in Year 4. Only Guyana was able to develop and implement wildlife management plans for hunting fishing including conservation at provincial level using adaptive management principles

title.narrative: Implemented approach to changing food behaviour of wildmeat consumers in the long term

description.narrative: An approach to changing food behaviour of urban and/or rural populations is deployed to reduce the consumption of unsustainable wild meat in favour of more sustainable or alternative domestic sources

title.narrative: % sites where planned evidencebased behaviour change campaigns that can influence offtake levels in WMUs managed by partner communities are organized

description.narrative: % sites where planned evidencebased behaviour change campaigns that can influence offtake levels in WMUs managed by partner communities are organized

comment.narrative: 0 site out of 5 potential sites involved in this approach Guyana Congo DRC Madagascar Gabon2020
By end of Y5 100 of the sites where it is deemed relevant have organized at least one campaign to change food behaviour based on the consumption information collected

In Year 4 there was significant progress in rolling out behavioural change campaigns in three out of the five sites that include this approach in their ToC i.e. 60 percent with campaigns planned in a fourth site In October 2021 the Madagascar team published an internal report outlining its behaviour change strategy. This aims to support the shift from subsistence use of vulnerable endemic species to that of resilient domestic or wild species. The low availability of domestic meat in the sites combined with the dietary importance of hunting and consuming wildmeat led to continued consumption of wild species including lemurs which are particularly vulnerable to overhunting. In December 2021 a meeting was held with the Coordinator of the Regional Nutrition Office of the Analanjirofo region to discuss avenues for collaboration. In Year 5 the campaign materials will be developed and the strategy rolled out to all project sites. Meanwhile the Breakfast programme is already underway and will continue in Year 5 aimed at raising awareness among the younger generations on the issues of nutrition and the wildlife conservation. In the Congo the SWM Programme team is designing a behaviour change campaign to reduce wildmeat consumption in Ouesso town following information from the consumption survey conducted there. In Year 4 the team completed a consumer lifestyle survey whose results were used to define the target population 1827yearolds and the preferred alternative chicken for the campaign. Additional informal interviews with the target audience are ongoing and the campaign strategy is now being prepared. A test campaign will be launched in Ouesso in Year 5. In Pokola logging camp the design of a campaign will begin starting with a consumer lifestyle survey and drawing on lessons from the Ouesso test. In April 2021 building on the behaviour change training given by an expert in conservationrelated behaviour change campaigns Brooke Tully the Guyana site team published their behavioural change strategy as an internal SWM Programme report. In Year 4 the team promoted the We love the Rupununi Wild campaign encouraging visitors and residents to protect wildlife and respect village rules with regard to wildlife use. Banners to promote sustainable hunting were placed in several locations across the main road from Annai to Aishalton in the Rupununi Region and at border locations. On the Coast a poster to discourage unsustainable hunting was placed in several restaurants and rum shops. In parallel the Local meat you cant beat campaign encourages the consumption of locally produced meat as an alternative to wildmeat discouraging the purchase of imported meats. Radio messages featuring Sabel the giant anteater were aired on local radio stations to promote wildlifefriendly behaviour among road users. The campaign needs to gain more strength on the Coast in Year 5 specifically discouraging the consumption of tapir and armadillos. In Gabon a social marketing consultant will be contracted in Year 5 to develop a strategy to change consumer behaviour to consume meat from sustainable sources. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo food consumption studies in urban areas Mambasa showed that there was a low consumption of animal proteins no real preference for wildmeat and a market for poultry. Behaviour change campaigns are therefore not seen as a priority. Similarly in Zambia and Zimbabwe this approach was deemed unnecessary following baseline assessments.

In the Congo the SWM Programme team is designing a behaviour change campaign to reduce wildmeat consumption in Ouesso town following information from the consumption survey conducted there. In Year 4 the team completed a consumer lifestyle survey whose results were used to define the target population 1827yearolds and the preferred alternative chicken for the campaign. Additional informal interviews with the target audience are ongoing and the campaign strategy is now being prepared. A test campaign will be launched in Ouesso in Year 5. In Pokola logging camp the design of a campaign will begin starting with a consumer lifestyle survey and drawing on lessons from the Ouesso test. In April 2021 building on the behaviour change training given by an expert in conservationrelated behaviour change campaigns Brooke Tully the Guyana site team published their behavioural change strategy as an internal SWM Programme report. In Year 4 the team promoted the We love the Rupununi Wild campaign encouraging visitors and residents to protect wildlife and respect village rules with regard to wildlife use. In Gabon a social marketing consultant will be contracted in Year 5 to develop a strategy to change consumer behaviour to consume meat from sustainable sources. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo food consumption studies in urban areas Mambasa showed that there was a low consumption of animal proteins no real preference for wildmeat and a market for poultry. comment.narrative: Site data management Online meetings of the data management taskforce have been carried out regularly to identify support needs for those engaged in data management and how to link data to MELIA plans the WILDMEAT project camera distance sampling GRM and hunting offtake. Hunting data In Gabon automation of hunting data processing chains using the Liste dOutils de Gestion Intgre de la Chasse LOGIC toolbox continued to be developed. In close collaboration with the Result 2 team a series of visualizations were generated for different types of audiences project facilitators local hunting associations administrations etc. The ambition is to produce an allinone tool that allows the management and monitoring of village hunting from data collection to decision support at the local level. An automated workflow has also been developed for hunting offtake data collected with KoBo Toolbox from the Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the WILDMEAT database by developing OpenFn scripts. Data are regularly being checked for new and updated submissions and automatically transferred to the WILDMEAT database for storage and analyses. Camera trapping data The two tools Wildlife Insights and Mbaza software tested to date have proven to be of limited addedvalue in accelerating species identification because the remote sites have a poor internet connection. In addition there are plans to incorporate distance sampling methods. Wildlife Insights however still provides an excellent repository for sharing data and promoting SWM Programme work. description.narrative: Developed and tested early detection and rapid response systems for zoonotic disease transmission along wild meat value chains

title.narrative: % of pilot countries where efforts for zoonotic risk assessment along wild meat value chainshave been carried out

description.narrative: % of countries where there isa) Availability of risk assessment studies along wild meat value chainsb) Biological sampling efforts for zoonotic pathogen detection in wildlife and humans

comment.narrative: N 3 countries as a minimun

In the Congo in order to develop and test a stepbystep evidencebased process for the practical implementation of tailored mitigation measures that take into account infectious disease risks conservation food security and livelihoods a preliminary literature review and analyses of existing data from the implementation partner including from SWM Programme market surveys was carried out on bats which represent reservoirs for many zoonotic RNA viruses. This work has allowed the identification of the actors in the value chain especially hunters who will be targeted by serum analyses to assess the level of transmission of zoonotic diseases. At the same time blood sampling on the three bat families Coronaviridae Filoviridae and Paramyxoviridae are being prepared International Review Board authorization training of technicians. In the Congo and Gabon surveys are being carried out the practices and perception of zoonotic risks in the wildmeat sector with a focus on bats in the Congo. The feasibility and acceptability of communitybased monitoring of zoonoses in the wildmeat sector was assessed in Gabon. In Guyana the SWM Programme initiated a process in collaboration with CBS to prioritize zoonotic diseases in Guyana.

comment.narrative: N 3 countries as a minimun

In the Congo in order to develop and test a stepbystep evidencebased process for the practical implementation of tailored mitigation measures that take into account infectious disease risks conservation food security and livelihoods a preliminary literature review and analyses of existing data from the implementation partner including from SWM Programme market surveys was carried out on bats which represent reservoirs for many zoonotic RNA viruses. This work has allowed the identification of the actors in the value chain especially hunters who will be targeted by serum analyses to assess the level of transmission of zoonotic diseases. At the same time blood sampling on the three bat families Coronaviridae Filoviridae and Paramyxoviridae are being prepared International Review Board authorization training of technicians. In the Congo and Gabon surveys are being carried out the practices and perception of zoonotic risks in the wildmeat sector with a focus on bats in the Congo. The feasibility and acceptability of communitybased monitoring of zoonoses in the wildmeat sector was assessed in Gabon. In Guyana the SWM Programme initiated a process in collaboration with CBS to prioritize zoonotic diseases in Guyana.

title.narrative: % sites with ToCbased monitoring, evaluation, learning and impact assessment (MELIA) plans developed and implemented

description.narrative: % sites with ToCbased monitoring, evaluation, learning and impact assessment (MELIA) plans developed and implemented

comment.narrative: Eight sites Gabon Congo Democratic Republic of the Congo PNG Guyana Madagascar KaZa Zimbabwe and Zambia out of ten sites have developed a sitespecific ToC that is regularly at least once a year being reviewed based on new knowledge and experience acquired from the implementation of activities. Botswana and Namibia are adapting existing ToCs but revised ToCs are not yet fully used to inform the MELIA system for these two sites. The RESSOURCE Project was not designed based on a ToC. However with training and facilitation support from Foundation of Success an endproject ToC has been designed in close collaboration with implementation partners which is being used to develop the extension of the of the project. The MTE considered the system too complex for an effective daily use by site coordinators and too heavy to be handled only by parttime staff at both the programme and site levels. Together with the R6 team a selfassessment was carried out on the key needs and issues through interviews with the different ME information users. The results of this selfassessment indicate that all site teams have acknowledged the ToC as a positive and powerful tool to engage with local stakeholders and build a common understanding of the rationale for the interventions. It was also deemed useful to maintain a consistent strategic direction despite frequent turnover in site team management staff across most sites. Finally participatory pause and reflect sessions to review the ToC have been generally appreciated and are now regularly being used for ToC review prior to annual work planning at most sites.

comment.narrative: 0 Inception

By end of Year 5 country profiles on the legal framework relevant to sustainable wildlife management with recommendations on priorities for improvement are available and online for at least 14 pilot countries.

The identification of priorities for legal improvements in relation to SWM models and objectives is specific to each countrysite and needs to be grounded on a commonshared understanding of the existing legal framework by the relevant stakeholders. This is often a challenge in the absence of the applicable legal texts and the time and skills that the average endusersstakeholders should have to analyse the content of all these instruments. To overcome these obstacles detailed legal analysis have been conducted based on specific tools T and methodologies M namely on the domestication of relevant international instruments TM and gap analysis across sectoral legislation TM the existing customary law TM and the barriers to implementation andor enforcement of laws TM. To date these analyses have been completed in nine countries i.e. Congo Chad Gabon Guyana Madagascar Mali Senegal Sudan and Zimbabwe and validated by the respective governments. This has led to the publication of a dedicated country page on the Legal Hub. The Guyana page is the first to also include a specific section on the existing customary law.

description.narrative: Number of management units legally established under appropriate formal contractual arrangements to enable communitybased SWM

comment.narrative: 61 WMUs already formally recognized inception 10 MDG 39 Guyana 12 Namibia 13 WMUs to be created under existing formal contractual arrangements for participatory wildlife management inception 10 Gabon and 3 PNG 7 WMUs to be created under existing legal arrangements that only allow partial community participation in wildlife management inception 1 ZW 2 Zambia 1 BW 2 DRC 1 Congo

By end of Y5 across all sites at least 20 new WMUs are legally constituted under appropriate formal contractual arrangements to enable communitybased SWM 61 existing ones are maintained and benefit from improved legal arrangements.

According to countries and pilot field sites the SWM Programme is at different stages of developing locally suitable CBSWM models. Three different circumstances are encountered1. CBSWM Units are already formally recognized under relevant contractual arrangements. But these arrangements or their application needs to be improved to allow effective devolution of exclusion and management rights to communities. This is the case for 61 established CBSWM Units that are supported by the SWM Programme including eight communauts de base grassroots communities COBAs and two zones doccupation contrles ZOCs controlled occupation zones in Madagascar 39 registered communityowned lands in Guyana and 12 CCs registered in Namibia.In Madagascar where the SWM Programme is working with local communities surrounding the Makira Natural Park they benefit from the transfer of natural resources management through contractual instruments. The Programme is currently supporting the local communities on the revision of seven of these instruments to better reflect the customary rules and practices that the local population deems necessary while also supporting the ten partner COBAsZOCs to renew these contracts while integrating sustainable wildlife management aspects.2. There are formal contractual arrangements allowing effective devolution of exclusionary and management rights to communities but they were yet to be implemented at the pilot sites at project launch with more or less significant adaptations to meet sustainable wildlife management goals. In total the creation of 13 CBSWM Units is targeted under these current arrangements ten community forests in Gabon and three SWM deeds in PNG.In PNG three SWM deeds were signed between registered community land owners at two sites Kwiop and Miruma.3. There is currently no formal contractual arrangement for the effective devolution of exclusionary and management rights to communities required for the proposed model. However there are other arrangements with partial community participationdevolution to communities that can be used as a short and intermediate term while legal reforms are encouraged for the effective uptake of appropriate arrangements in the longer term. In total the creation of seven CBSWM Units is targeted under these existing arrangements one CC in Botswana one CC in Zimbabwe two CCs in Zambia one adapted community development zone in Kabo logging sustainable forest management unit in the Congo and two community hunting zones in the Okapi Wildlife Reserve OWR in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.In Botswana after developing a draft bill on community based natural resources management the SWM Programme is working towards identifying an interim solution to enable wildlife management by communities pending the enactment of the bill.As in Botswana in Zimbabwe although the communities can participate as beneficiaries to conservancies run by statutory institutions they cannot autonomously manage the conservancy since there is no legal recognition of their status as appropriate authorities. In this regard the SWM Programme works towards extending this status to local communities in the Parks and Wildlife Act and its enabling instruments so that they can run their conservancies autonomously for the development of residents and the sustainable use of wildlife and tourismIn the Democratic Republic of the Congo the SWM Programme is also defining a set of agreed rules Access to Natural Resources Guidelines or DARN to guide and regulate wildlife hunting by local communities within the whole OWR.

comment.narrative: 61 WMUs already formally recognized inception 10 MDG 39 Guyana 12 Namibia 13 WMUs to be created under existing formal contractual arrangements for participatory wildlife management inception 10 Gabon and 3 PNG 7 WMUs to be created under existing legal arrangements that only allow partial community participation in wildlife management inception 1 ZW 2 Zambia 1 BW 2 DRC 1 Congo

By end of Y5 across all sites at least 20 new WMUs are legally constituted under appropriate formal contractual arrangements to enable communitybased SWM 61 existing ones are maintained and benefit from improved legal arrangements.

According to countries and pilot field sites the SWM Programme is at different stages of developing locally suitable CBSWM models. Three different circumstances are encountered1. CBSWM Units are already formally recognized under relevant contractual arrangements. But these arrangements or their application needs to be improved to allow effective devolution of exclusion and management rights to communities. This is the case for 61 established CBSWM Units that are supported by the SWM Programme including eight communauts de base grassroots communities COBAs and two zones doccupation contrles ZOCs controlled occupation zones in Madagascar 39 registered communityowned lands in Guyana and 12 CCs registered in Namibia.In Madagascar where the SWM Programme is working with local communities surrounding the Makira Natural Park they benefit from the transfer of natural resources management through contractual instruments. The Programme is currently supporting the local communities on the revision of seven of these instruments to better reflect the customary rules and practices that the local population deems necessary while also supporting the ten partner COBAsZOCs to renew these contracts while integrating sustainable wildlife management aspects.2. There are formal contractual arrangements allowing effective devolution of exclusionary and management rights to communities but they were yet to be implemented at the pilot sites at project launch with more or less significant adaptations to meet sustainable wildlife management goals. In total the creation of 13 CBSWM Units is targeted under these current arrangements ten community forests in Gabon and three SWM deeds in PNG.In PNG three SWM deeds were signed between registered community land owners at two sites Kwiop and Miruma.3. There is currently no formal contractual arrangement for the effective devolution of exclusionary and management rights to communities required for the proposed model. However there are other arrangements with partial community participationdevolution to communities that can be used as a short and intermediate term while legal reforms are encouraged for the effective uptake of appropriate arrangements in the longer term. In total the creation of seven CBSWM Units is targeted under these existing arrangements one CC in Botswana one CC in Zimbabwe two CCs in Zambia one adapted community development zone in Kabo logging sustainable forest management unit in the Congo and two community hunting zones in the Okapi Wildlife Reserve OWR in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.In Botswana after developing a draft bill on community based natural resources management the SWM Programme is working towards identifying an interim solution to enable wildlife management by communities pending the enactment of the bill.As in Botswana in Zimbabwe although the communities can participate as beneficiaries to conservancies run by statutory institutions they cannot autonomously manage the conservancy since there is no legal recognition of their status as appropriate authorities. In this regard the SWM Programme works towards extending this status to local communities in the Parks and Wildlife Act and its enabling instruments so that they can run their conservancies autonomously for the development of residents and the sustainable use of wildlife and tourismIn the Democratic Republic of the Congo the SWM Programme is also defining a set of agreed rules Access to Natural Resources Guidelines or DARN to guide and regulate wildlife hunting by local communities within the whole OWR.

description.narrative: Participating countries develop and adopt or improve their institutional, legal and/or regulatory frameworks to ensure the maintenance of wildlife populations for ecosystem integrity and ecological services, including the sustainable use of wildlife by rights holders at target sites

title.narrative: Number of pilot countries with ongoing participatory processes to mitigate legal weaknesses and gaps and enable sustainable wildlife management

description.narrative: Number of pilot countries where the programme supports participatory processes aiming at mitigating legal weaknesses and gaps identified as priorities on the basis of evidence at national and site level

comment.narrative: All countries have set priorities in line with their respective models at both site and national level

By end of Year 5 the SWM Programme will have provided the relevant authorities with proposals for new andor improved legislation based on evidence and participatory processes for at least 80 of the identified priorities in at least 6 of the pilot countries

In countries where the legal analysis has been completed they have triggered legislative work on identified priorities to enable the sustainable management of wildlife. In Botswana this has triggered the drafting of a Communitybased Natural Resources Management Bill which has already included field consultations with local communities as well as a bilateral review with the Ministry of Environment. However following a ministerial reorganization the SWM Programme is following up with the new officials on the promulgation of the bill. In Madagascar the SWM Programme analysis has led to the revision of Ordinance No. 60126 which sets out the hunting fishing and wildlife protection regime in the country. This work is being carried out in liaison with the Ministre de lEnvironnement et du Dveloppement Durable Ministry of the Environment and Sustainable Development that has set up a multistakeholder working group which is also using the Legal Hub for dialogue with all stakeholders public sector private sector nongovernmental organizations and associations to achieve its specific mandate. Similar initiatives are also ongoing in the Congo Guyana and Zimbabwe where the SWM Programme has provided its support in the review of sectoral legislations that have been identified as priority i.e. wildlife law in the Congo Parks and Wildlife Act in Zimbabwe and fisheries regulations in Guyana. In Zimbabwe the contribution has been indirect by building the capacity of the stakeholders involved in the law reform process. In Guyana the SWM Programme has and still is directly contributing to the drafting of fisheries regulations.

title.narrative: Number of pilot countries with improved access to legal texts relevant to sustainable wildlife management

description.narrative: Number of pilot countries where stakeholders at national level can have improved access to the legal texts relevant to sustainable wildlife management

comment.narrative: Available in Congo 2019 DRC 2019 MDG 2018 Guyana 2018 ZW 2020 Zambia 2021 PNG 2020 Gabon 2020 Senegal Mali Chad Sudan Suriname 2021 Indicator exists but no baseline available yet in Botswana BW Namibia
By end of Year 5 at least 14 target countries have 100 of identified texts in force uploaded to an online legal platform.

With a few exceptions the countries where the SWM Programme works have no regular publication of an Official Gazette and no updated online service for accessing legal instruments. This represents a major barrier for legal information in the country for the average individual including across the sectors relevant to the sustainable management of wildlife. FAOLEX as the major legislative and policy database is also struggling to remain updated over time. Through support of national legal consultants all available legal instruments in 13 countries where the Programme operates have been gathered to date often in hard copy from the relevant ministries. All the texts gathered have been catalogued using a specific methodology developed for this very purpose and organized by sector into a matrix Annex 1 in consideration of their hierarchy. All these texts have progressively been shared with FAOLEX for their upload and processed for 14 countries Botswana Republic of the Congo Democratic Republic of the Congo Egypt Gabon Guyana Madagascar Mali Senegal Sudan Suriname Chad Zambia and Zimbabwe. Moreover the relevant legal texts have also been made available on the dedicated page of the respective Legal Hubs for 10 of these OACPS countries Madagascar Zimbabwe Gabon Senegal Republic of the Congo Mali Guyana Mali Sudan and Chad. The Legal Hub has attracted considerable attention and dramatically increased the visitors to the SWM Programme web portal.

description.narrative: Existence of strategic partnerships and collaborations established at national and supranational levels

comment.narrative: Conservation Social Science Partnership The collaboration with Conservation Social Science ConSoSci contributes to promoting sustaining and scaling SWM Programme best practices for BNS and NGRT survey methods. This allows the teams to benefit from automated workflow for consumption and offtake data and to identify opportunities to simplify enhance and scale up data collection using ConSoSci tools. Wildmeat project and database In Year 4 by sharing SWM site wildmeat data in the WILDMEAT database the data continued to be accessible and useful to others for analyses. The SWM Programme has contributed to regionallevel WILDMEAT data analyses through 80 percent funding of a postdoctoral position. In addition discussions have begun between the SWM Programme and the WILDMEAT project to create wildmeat indicators for use at the site national and international levels. As a follow up in May 2022 the SWM Programme in collaboration with WILDMEAT Oxford University UKRI TRADE Hub TRAFFIC USFWS and USAID held a twoday indicators workshop to further develop indicators at these three levels. As a result the SWM Programme is now part of the TRAFFICled expert working group to develop indicators for the post2020 Convention on Biological Diversity CBD Targets. These discussions continued in June 2022 during a oneday symposium at the 2022 European Tropical Ecology Conference followed by a halfday meeting of Central African researchers at CIRAD to discuss indicators at the site level and share lessons learned. Wildlife Insight The partnership with the platform is still of interest but mostly for secondary purposes until there are concrete and feasible ways to improve the platform to meet SWM Programme needs.

comment.narrative: The SWM Programme carried out a series of activities targeting project staff across ten sites Gabon Democratic Republic of the Congo Madagascar Guyana Zimbabwe Zambia PNG Namibia Botswana following the CRBA including Indigenous Peoples and local communities right to Free Prior and Informed Consent FPIC. This was achieved through the development of a wide range of framework documents in particular sitespecific FPIC protocols adapted to the local contexts to ensure that local communities and the Indigenous Peoples with whom it engages are involved in decisionmaking regarding any project activity that may affect them. As of 31 July 2022 FPIC agreements were signed in six SWM Programme sites where the involved of the communities ranged from 74 percent i.e. Guyana to 100 percent i.e. Gabon Congo Madagascar and PNG. In order to enhance community awareness on their rights and to ensure consistency across the SWM Programme staff on the FPIC approach a set of communication materials was produced and used by project staff with the local communities e.g. posters banners and a short animation explaining FPIC and the participatory process. The video is available on YouTube in English and French and was also produced in Swahili Tonga and Lingala and is being translated into Lozi. The FPIC posters are also available in different languages and illustrate the main steps to implement FPIC Free English French Swahili Tonga Tsimihety Betsimisaraka Prior English French SwahiliTonga Tsimihety Betsimisaraka Informed English French SwahiliTonga Tsimihety Betsimisaraka Consent English French Swahili Tonga Tsimihety Betsimisaraka. In May 2022 an FPIC training was specifically delivered to staff members in Madagascar. The Forest Peoples Programme provided training and coaching to site teams with a focus on FPIC processes at SWM Programme sites in the Central Africa region 11 people trained in Gabon Congo Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2019. One of the major successful outcomes is the official validation in June 2021 of the SWM Programme FPIC process by the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights and Promotion of Indigenous Peoples of the Congo. This is the first FPIC process to be successfully validated in the country.

comment.narrative: The SWM Programme GRM aims to ensure that any projectrelated complaints for violation of the FAO Environmental and Social Standards made by individuals or groups of people are resolved in an effective timely and transparent manner. The SWM Programme developed a specific framework for GRM with support from the FAO Office of the Inspector General. To date four sites have finalized or are finalizing their GRMs including through electronic GRM protocols by Asana. Guyana has already developed a sitespecific GRM as well as a GRM brochure for partners and community representatives. In addition in the Democratic Republic of the Congo a hotline in local languages was developed to increase access to the GRM in the OWR which covers a population of 4 500 women and men across three villages. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo the communities of Epulu Eboyo and Bapukeli sent a letter of complaint to the SWM Programme Coordinator in Okapi about the incomegenerating and alternative protein production activities which have experienced significant delays. The issue was resolved through several consultations and discussions with the communities to gain a better understanding of their concerns. The consultations resulted in the codevelopment of alternative protein activities with the communities beans and poultry farming. In all other SWM sites where a GRM is functional no complaints regarding the SWM Programme and its implementing activities have been registered to date.

comment.narrative: The SWM Programme has involved local populations in the implementation of activities since its beginning. The empowerment of women men boys and girls of local communities and their participation in project activities are at its core. In this regard support has been provided to increase the active participation of women and men ethnic minorities and marginalized groups and their equal access to resources services and decisionmaking processes including FPIC and GRM mechanisms. The SWM programme developed a Template Situation Analysis to adapt the CRBA to the specifics of the SWM Programme sites models of sustainable wildlife management and projects workplans. The form is filled out based on the human rights information available at the nationalsite level. As of 31 July 2022 seven sites Gabon Congo Democratic Republic of the Congo Madagascar Guyana Zimbabwe PNG have developed sitespecific CRBA analysis. Specific support has been provided on how to mainstream gender into implementing activities throughout the project cycle from the design to the ME system. This includes the design of baseline gendersensitive surveys technical assistance in developing gender strategies and technical support for gender mainstreaming in specific tools e.g. BNS letters of agreement and the formulation of gendersensitive indicators. For example in the Congo gender focus groups were set up and a gender assessment was carried out. This assessment which combined national data and field information collected by the SWM Programme team revealed important information on the role of women in the wildmeat value chain. It showed that in the Ouesso Basin most wildmeat sellers such as wholesalers importers exporters and restaurateurs are female. In Zimbabwe women are included in local governance structures that preside over livestock production and marketing. The inclusion of women not only eliminates a traditional imbalance but also empowers them to provide food for their families directly. Finally in PNG a gender assessment in collaboration with CARE was conducted and gender equity and diversity training sessions were organized. During the training both men and women discussed the importance of communication and learned about the wide variety of skills needed to function effectively in a diverse and complex community group and workplace. Open discussions contributed to a better understanding of gender and diversity particularly of how gender fits into the cultural diversity of PNG. A brochure on the SWM Programme Gender Approach was developed and published in English and French. Moreover a web article on the gender approach was written and published in October 2021 by the European Commissions Capacity4dev. Finally a poster on the CRBA SoS tools achievements and first lessons learned for the World Forestry Congress 2022 was produced in English and French. In November 2021 training on SoS in the SWM Programme including gender mainstreaming was conducted at the community level in Guyana. In January 2022 training on Gender and Gender Mainstreaming in the SWM Programme was conducted remotely in Madagascar for gender focal points and other project staff members. In January 2022 and in March 2022 two pause and reflect events on gender and gender mainstreaming in the SWM Programme were respectively organized for Francophone sites and for Anglophone sites. Numerous staff from headquarters and sites participated in the events as well as in specific sessions that were dedicated to group work focused on taking stock the genderrelated activities carried out to date as well as planning genderrelated activities in each site for the next months. In July 2022 the first gender story as part of a series of web stories on gender and womens empowerment was produced by the Guyana team.

comment.narrative: Field teams responsible for carrying out surveys which involve interviewing people are trained in research ethics respect for interviewees rights and personal security especially for surveys on sensitive topics. Prior to any survey or study involving interviews the research protocols are reviewed by either an internal or an external ethical board. The achievements as of 31 July 2022 are as follows In eight sites where individual or household surveys were conducted i.e. Gabon Congo Democratic Republic of the Congo Madagascar Guyana Zimbabwe Zambia Papua New Guinea PNG the data collection followed internal or external ethical review processes set out in the protocols for conducting research on human subjects. The data collection was drawn from different surveys that are part of the SWM Programme activities e.g. surveys relating to value chain analysis urban consumption rural consumption activity diversification application of the law fishing market and basic necessity customary law animal production edible insects meat consumption and HWC. Several training sessions on Ethical Research Practices i.e. the Complete Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative CITI were carried in six countries Gabon Congo Democratic Republic of the Congo Madagascar Zimbabwe and PNG. For example about 50 people were trained in the Congo and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo while in Madagascar 25 people were trained. Finally every time a new surveyor staff member or intern begins hisher assignment training on Ethical Research Practices is provided to the entire team and also light ethic training sessions are run prior to each survey training.
